payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=longitudinal+preference+stability+in+multi-agent+reinforcement+learning+non-stationary+environments&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.4123080\", \"title\": [\"Context Detection and Identification in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning on Non-Stationary Environments\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Although the real world is non-stationary, most reinforcement learning algorithms are based on the assumption that the environment is stationary. Non-stationary environments are composed of several different stationary components (i.e., sub-environments or contexts). Therefore, algorithms that accept this assumption are incapable of learning within non-stationary environments. Reinforcement Learning - Context Detection (RL-CD) da Silva et al. (2016) method allows agents to learn the environment, detect context change points, and learn the partial model of the context without previous knowledge of the environment. RL-CD is a single-agent algorithm and it has shortcomings in learning within a multi-agent environment. In this work, we introduce a new method called Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning - Context Detection (MARL-CD), which can both detect context change points and enable agents to learn within non-stationary environments with multi-agent settings. This approach is based on RL-CD and works more effectively in terms of detecting context changes caused by agents and changes caused by the environment’s dynamics. It detects not only the change points originating from the environment, but also the change points created by the agents. Experimentally, agents spend 16% less energy compared to RL-CD and can detect change points more accurately and earlier.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4123080\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295\", \"title\": [\"Reinforcement learning in non-stationary environments\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Apprentissage par renforcement en environement non stationnaire</jats:title>\\n                <jats:p xml:lang=\\\"fr\\\">Comment un agent doit-il agir étant donné que son environnement évolue de manièreincertaine ? Dans cette thèse, nous fournissons une réponse à cette question du point devue de l’apprentissage par renforcement. Le problème est vu sous trois aspects différents.Premièrement, nous étudions le compromis planification vs. re-planification des algorithmesde recherche arborescente dans les Processus Décisionnels Markoviens. Nous proposons uneméthode pour réduire la complexité de calcul d’un tel algorithme, tout en conservant desguaranties théoriques sur la performance. Deuxièmement, nous étudions le cas des environnementsévoluant graduellement au cours du temps. Cette hypothèse est formulée dansun cadre mathématique appelé Processus de Décision Markoviens Non-Stationnaires Lipschitziens.Dans ce cadre, nous proposons un algorithme de planification robuste aux évolutionspossibles, dont nous montrons qu’il converge vers la politique minmax. Troisièmement,nous considérons le cas de l’évolution temporelle abrupte dans le cadre du “lifelong learning”(apprentissage tout au long de la vie). Nous proposons une méthode de transfert non-négatifbasée sur l’étude théorique de la continuité de Lipschitz de la Q-fonction optimale par rapportà l’espace des tâches. L’approche permet d’accélérer l’apprentissage dans de nouvelles tâches.Dans l’ensemble, cette dissertation propose des réponses à la question de la résolution desProcessus de Décision Markoviens Non-Stationnaires dans trois cadres d’hypothèses.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7404755\", \"title\": [\"Tracking Non-Stationary Equilibria in Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Evolutionary Dynamics\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Non-stationarity is a fundamental challenge in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). It arises from the continuous and simultaneous learning of multiple agents: as each agent adapts its policy, the environment dynamics change over time, continuously shifting the equilibria. This problem is further compounded when the learning dynamics themselves are inherently non-stationary. Evolutionary game theory (EGT) offers a complementary perspective on this challenge by studying how strategies evolve within a population over time. However, existing work combining EGT with MARL remains limited to simple, tabular settings, and consequently fails to exploit the scalability of deep reinforcement learning.We introduce Deep Evolutionary Dynamics (DeepED), a novel actor-critic MARL algorithm that integrates evolutionary game theory into deep reinforcement learning. Instead of directly optimising policies towards expected returns, DeepED leverages critic-based fitness estimates to generate an evolutionary target policy via evolutionary dynamics, and the actor policy is then updated to track this target.On the theoretical side, we establish a dynamical regret bound for DeepED. Furthermore, we prove that the value gap between the Nash value and the current expected value follows a contraction of a quadratic form.Beyond the theoretical analysis, we evaluate DeepED across three levels of progressively increasing complexity: matrix games, gridworld environments and VMAS tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that DeepED tracks shifting equilibria more accurately and stably than prominent baselines such as QMIX, MAPPO and IPPO. Ultimately, these results show that DeepED successfully extends evolutionary principles beyond simple games to challenging, high-dimensional settings.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7404755\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223\", \"title\": [\"Non-Stationary Policy Learning for Multi-Timescale Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023, 12, 13]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "4d835bc87a39e027835cda87b95ae1cf5ced978fddcac1e185d1dba251016647", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.4123080", "doi:10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7404755", "doi:10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4123080", "https://doi.org/10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7404755", "https://doi.org/10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
